title: Why second-guessing competitors is a losing game: build the best company for yourself
summary: Using Rock, Paper, Scissors as an analogy, Jason Cohen shows how trying to outguess what competitors know and think leads to endless recursive fakes. His startup takeaway is to stop reacting to rivals and instead focus inward on building something you're proud of for your customers.

principles.text: Don't try to outwit competitors; do your best work directly for your customers.
principles.quote: Even better than trying to outwit the competition, is to not react to them at all, and just do your best, directly for your customers.

principles.text: Second-guessing competitors' knowledge and reactions is an endless recursion with no stable answer.
principles.quote: This is like trying to second-guess what your competitors think, what they know, what they think they know, whether they'll react to your knowledge of that guess, etc..

principles.text: Build the best company you can for yourself, and focus inward rather than on rivals.
principles.quote: In the end, screw it, just build the best company you can, for you.

principles.text: Your beliefs about competitors, good and bad, are mostly wrong, so build something you're proud of.
principles.quote: You're wrong about most of what you think about those competitors anyway--both the good and bad--so focus inward, and build something you're proud of.

principles.text: In an adversarial game, whoever has more information wins more often, though every edge gets countered once known.
principles.quote: That, at least in regard to this study, people with more information win more often.
